source.title: MESH: Scaling Up Retrieval with Heterogeneous Content Unification
source.authors: Jia-Xing Qu; Yi-Lin Chen; Jun-Peng Hou; Jin-Feng Rao; Olafur Gudmundsson; Sai Xiao; Hui-Zhong Duan

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in industrial recommendation retrieval, a different model domain and task from text-pretraining language models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports recommendation-recall scaling sweeps and fitted exponents, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. Its results bear on V5 as a different training/task domain. It does not test language-model loss extrapolation or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Online engagement and serving results are not rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws (y = αx^β + γ) of offline Recall against FLOPs or parameter count for two-tower recommendation retrieval models. It reports exponents per content segment for a flat baseline and for MESH. This bears on V5 (the power-law form outside text pretraining), but the measure is a retrieval metric, not loss, and the compute range is narrow.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that flat unified retrieval architectures show a 'Scaling Bias of Heterogeneity': capacity gains go mainly to evergreen content (β 0.0274 versus 0.0059 for fresh). MESH's modular design raises the fresh exponent about 14× (to 0.0826) and this translates into online gains on fresh and long-tail segments. They claim this as structural, not fixable by brute-force capacity.
record.recipe_differences: An industrial two-tower recommendation retrieval study using Recall@100 and content-segment scaling fits, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported scaling exponents differ by content segment and architecture; the fresh-content exponent drops in the listed MESH ablations.

fits_no_version.finding: In recsys retrieval, ablating MESH components changes the fresh-segment scaling exponent drastically (0.0826 to 0.0071 without semantic amplifiers, to 0.0528 without the modular backbone, to 0.0645 without RGBC). Separately, per-group gradient norm ratios fall from 12.4× to 4.7×.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation models, the scaling exponent depends strongly on architecture and on the data segment evaluated (architecture-dependent scaling exponents outside text pretraining).

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems; accepted RecSys 2026 Industry Track
record.problems: The evidence uses proprietary Pinterest data and recommendation recall rather than language-model pretraining loss. The text says Table 2 scaling evaluations show five independent evaluations, but does not give uncertainty for the individual table values; only the fresh MESH exponent has a stated bootstrap interval.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported results bearing on the tested version were left out. Online engagement, funnel, retention, and serving-efficiency results were excluded because they do not measure the scaling form named by V5.

untested.parts: Only recommendation retrieval with Recall metrics (not loss) is examined. The compute range is narrow (about 2 to 11 TFLOPs; 7.3M to 328M params). No goodness-of-fit is shown. Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested, and there is no data or token scaling.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
Not tested: no compute-optimal parameter/data allocation.
Not tested for language models. Recsys width/depth sweeps confound shape with parameter count.
Not tested: online A/B metrics are not related to scale or loss.
Not tested for language-model scaling laws. Exponents differ by segment and architecture, but this is recsys retrieval.

missing.what: Individual data points, compute range and fit quality behind the Figure 2 segment-wise power-law fits (only the exponents are reported in text). Needed to judge whether the power-law form actually holds.

Online A/B comparison against RankMixer at two scales (28M and 135M): the larger flat model widens the fresh-repin gap versus MESH (−1.42% to −2.99%). This is relevant context for flat-architecture scaling on sparse content.

record.verdict_notes: Recall is a retrieval metric, not a loss. Exponents are tiny, and the compute spans well under one order of magnitude, so this is weak evidence on the power-law form. Table 2 is labelled Recall@100 while the text discusses Recall@10. Most scaling rows are the study's own method (MESH). Only the flat-baseline exponents (r13, r14) describe a standard architecture.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of language-model loss from smaller runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between parameter count and training tokens.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count for language-model loss.
Only recommendation retrieval is examined, using Recall metrics rather than language-model pretraining loss. Image/video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
Predictability of language-model downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.

The paper reports different exponents across recommendation content segments and architectures, but does not test language-model fitting choices or whether language-model loss curves depart from a single power law.

relationships.condition: Recommendation retrieval, MESH architecture (both segments) and flat baseline on evergreen content
relationships.reason: Positive fitted power-law exponents are reported: MESH fresh β=0.0826 (bootstrap CI 0.0772–0.0874), MESH evergreen 0.0160, flat evergreen 0.0274 (r13, r15, r16). Recall rises monotonically with diminishing returns in the capacity sweeps (r2, r3, r6–r8, r10–r12). Range is narrow and fit quality is not shown.
relationships.display_finding: Recall rose monotonically with diminishing returns, with fitted exponents of 0.0826 for MESH fresh content (bootstrap confidence interval 0.0772–0.0874), 0.0160 for MESH evergreen content and 0.0274 for flat evergreen retrieval, although the scaling range was narrow and fit quality was unreported.

relationships.condition: Flat architecture on sparse/fresh content; large-d end of the MESH sweep
relationships.reason: The flat baseline's fresh-content exponent is nearly stagnant (β=0.0059, r14), so scaling strength depends on data segment and architecture. Recall saturates when going from d=64 to d=128 despite more than double the params (r4).
relationships.display_finding: The flat baseline's fresh-content exponent was only 0.0059, while MESH recall saturated from dimension 64 to 128 despite more than doubling parameters.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
